Abstract
In the past years, multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have demonstrated remarkable performance in tasks
such as visual question answering and visual understanding and reasoning. However, the extensive model size and
high training and inference costs have hindered the widespread application of MLLMs in academia and industry.
Thus, studying eﬃcient and lightweight MLLMs has enormous potential, especially in edge computing scenarios. In
this survey, we provide a comprehensive and systematic review of the current state of eﬃcient MLLMs. Speciﬁcally,
this survey summarizes the timeline of representative eﬃcient MLLMs, the current state of research in structures and
strategies, and the applications. Finally, the limitations of current eﬃcient MLLM research and promising future
directions are discussed.
Keywords: Eﬃciency, Multi-modal large language lodel (MLLM), Instruction tuning, Vision token compression
1 Introduction
Large-scale pretraining, a leading approach in artiﬁcial
intelligence (AI), has demonstrated that general-purpose
models, such as large language and multimodal mod-
els, outperform specialized deep learning models across
various tasks. The remarkable capabilities of large lan-
guage models (LLMs) have spurred eﬀorts to integrate
them with other modality-based models to enhance mul-
timodal competencies. This concept is further validated
by the success of proprietary models such as OpenAI’s
GPT-4V [1] and Google’s Gemini [2]. As a result, mul-
timodal large language models (MLLMs) have emerged,
including the mPLUG-Owl series [3, 4], InternVL [5],
the Qwen-VL series [6], EMU [7], LLaVA [8], Instruct-
BLIP [9], MiniGPT-v2 [10], and MiniGPT-4 [11]. The de-
velopment of more compact and eﬃcient MLLMs, such
as Mini-InternVL [12], has further accelerated progress in
this domain. MLLMs inherit the cognitive capabilities of

mainstream MLLMs, represented by GPT-4V and Gemini,
are controlled by a few dominant corporations and operate
in the cloud environment. Moreover, the diﬃculty of de-
ploying MLLMs on edge devices further exacerbates the
challenges associated with ensuring equitable access and
preserving user privacy.
A crucial question then arises: do the pathways for ef-
ﬁcient MLLMs simply boil down to those for eﬃcient
LLMs? While there is a signiﬁcant overlap, we argue that
research into eﬃcient MLLMs addresses a distinct set of
challenges that are not present in the text-only domain.
First, MLLMs introduce a substantial computational over-
head from the vision encoder, which must process high-
dimensional inputs like images. Second, and more criti-
cally, is the challenge of cross-modal fusion. A standard-
resolution image is often converted into hundreds or even
thousands of visual tokens. When these are concatenated
with text tokens and fed into the LLM, the total sequence
length surges, causing the computational cost of the self-
attention mechanism—which is quadratic in sequence
length—to become a primary bottleneck. Therefore, a sig-
niﬁcant portion of research on eﬃcient MLLMs focuses
on MLLM-speciﬁc problems such as designing lightweight
vision-language connectors and, most importantly, com-
pressing the vast number of visual tokens before they are
processed by the LLM. These challenges are unique to the
multimodal architecture and are largely orthogonal to the
methods for making the LLM backbone itself more eﬃ-
cient. This highlights the necessity for a dedicated survey
to systematically organize and analyze these unique eﬃ-
ciency strategies.
In light of these challenges, there has been a growing fo-
cus on the study of eﬃcient MLLMs, the timeline of which
is shown in Fig. 1. The eﬃciency of a MLLM is generally
determined by two factors: memory demand and inference
speed. However, reducing the model size inevitably leads
to a decline in performance and a loss of generalization
capabilities. The requirement for fast inference speed also
constrains the application scope of eﬃcient MLLMs. Con-
sequently, striking a balance between eﬃciency and capac-
ity has become the primary challenge and diﬃculty in the
research of eﬃcient MLLMs. The primary objective of re-
lated endeavors is to decrease the resource consumption of
MLLMs and broaden their applicability while minimizing
performance degradation.

Research on eﬃcient MLLMs began with replacing large
language models with lightweight counterparts and per-
forming typical visual instruction tuning [13–15], yet fail-
ing to yield satisfying results. This shows that the paths
for eﬃcient MLLMs cannot simply boil down to those
for eﬃcient LLMs. While eﬃcient LLM techniques pro-
vide foundational optimizations, eﬃcient MLLMs require
distinct approaches for three key reasons: (1) Visual-
language alignment: MLLMs require lightweight vision
encoders (e.g., ViTamin, BRAVE) and eﬃcient projectors
(e.g., LDPv2 [16], VSS [17]) to bridge modality gaps, the
design of which is absent in pure LLM optimization. (2)
Limitation of Transformer models: Transformers face a
unique computational challenge with images, as their cost
scales quadratically with the number of visual tokens. This
has spurred vision-speciﬁc compression techniques such
as S2-Wrapper [18] and LLaVA-UHD [19]—a problem ir-
relevant to text-based LLMs. (3) Joint modality optimiza-
tion: Techniques like MoE-LLaVA’s sparse gating [20] and
Cobra’s Mamba integration [21] optimize both language
and visual processing simultaneously, unlike LLM-only
strategies. While surveys on eﬃcient LLMs (e.g., [22]) ex-
ist, this work uniquely focuses on multimodal-speciﬁc ef-
ﬁciency trade-oﬀs, such as balancing visual feature ﬁdelity
with inference speed, which cannot be addressed by LLM-
only insights.
Subsequent studies further enhanced capabilities and
expanded use cases in the following ways: (1) Lighter archi-
tectures were introduced with an emphasis on eﬃciency,
aiming to reduce the number of parameters or computa-
tional complexity [17, 20, 21]; (2) More specialized com-
ponents were developed, focusing on eﬃciency optimiza-
tions tailored to advanced architectures or imbuing spe-
ciﬁc properties, such as locality [16, 23, 24]; and (3) Sup-
port for resource-sensitive tasks was provided, with some
works employing visual token compression to boost ef-
ﬁciency, enabling the transfer of MLLM capabilities to
resource-intensive tasks such as high-resolution (HR) im-
age and video understanding [18, 19, 25, 26].
Currently, there are only a few existing surveys available
on MLLMs [27–29]. For the ﬁrst time, this paper presents
an exhaustive organization of the recent advancements in
the rapidly evolving ﬁeld of eﬃcient MLLMs, as depicted
in Fig. 2. We organize the literature in a taxonomy con-
sisting of six primary categories, encompassing various as-
pects of eﬃcient MLLMs: architecture, eﬃcient vision, ef-
ﬁcient LLMs, training, data and benchmarks, and applica-
tions.
1) Architecture focuses on the MLLM framework devel-
oped by eﬃcient techniques to reduce the computa-
tional cost. The architecture is composed of multi-
ple modality-based fundamental models, that exhibit
characteristics distinct from those of single-modal
models, thus promoting the development of novel
technologies.
2) Eﬃcient vision explores optimizing eﬃcient visual
feature extraction strategies, emphasizing methods
that boost eﬃciency while maintaining accuracy. It
addresses integrating high-quality visual data for ef-
fective cross-modal understanding.
3) Eﬃcient LLMs explore these strategies of improving
the computational eﬃciency and scalability of lan-
guage models. This section examines the trade-oﬀs
between model complexity and performance while
suggesting promising avenues for balancing these
competing factors.
4) Training surveys the landscape of training method-
ologies that are pivotal in the development of eﬃ-
cient MLLMs. It addresses the challenges associated
with the pre-training stage, instruction-tuning stage,
and the overall training strategy for state-of-the-art
results.
5) Eﬃciency-aware data and benchmarks evaluate the
eﬃciency of datasets and benchmarks used in the
evaluation of multimodal language models. It assesses
the trade-oﬀs between dataset size, complexity, and
computational cost, while advocating for the devel-
opment of benchmarks that prioritize eﬃciency and
relevance to real-world applications.
6) Application investigates the practical implications of
eﬃcient MLLMs in various domains, emphasizing
the balance between performance and computational
cost. By addressing resource-intensive tasks such
as HR image understanding and medical question-
answering, this section highlights the potential of ef-
ﬁcient MLLMs to broaden their application scope and
contribute to real-world problem-solving.
To provide a clear and structured overview, this survey
is organized to reﬂect the composite nature of MLLMs.
An MLLM fundamentally consists of a vision encoder, a
language model, and a projector to connect them. There-
fore, creating an eﬃcient MLLM necessitates optimiz-
ing one or more of these core components. Our sur-
vey follows this logic. We begin in Sect. 2 by discussing
the overall architecture of eﬃcient MLLMs, covering the
interplay between these components. We then dedicate
Sect. 3 (eﬃcient vision) and Sect. 4 (eﬃcient LLMs) to
a more in-depth exploration of the speciﬁc techniques
for optimizing the vision and language modules, respec-
tively, as these represent the most signiﬁcant computa-
tional costs. This hierarchical structure, reﬂected in our
taxonomies, is designed to clearly establish the connection
between optimizing the parts and achieving eﬃciency in
the whole.
In summary, this survey explores various strategies for
making MLLMs more resource-eﬃcient. It reviews the
development history of eﬃcient MLLMs, provides a tax-
onomy of the strategies for eﬃcient MLLMs, and com-

2.1 Vision encoder
Taking the input image Xv as input, the vision encoder g
compresses the original image into more compact patch
features Zv, as represented by Eq. (1):
Zv = g(Xv).
(1)
In line with mainstream MLLM practices, eﬃcient
MLLMs select pre-trained models that are semantically
aligned with the text, represented by CLIP [80]. This ap-
proach facilitates better alignment between the feature
spaces of visual and text inputs. Since the vision encoder
constitutes a relatively minor portion of the MLLM pa-
rameters, the advantages of lightweight optimization are
less pronounced compared to the language model. There-
fore, eﬃcient MLLMs generally continue to employ visual
encoders that are widely used in large-scale MLLMs, as
detailed in Table 1.
However, the choice of vision encoder is crucial for bal-
ancing eﬃciency and capability. For instance, models such
as EVA [87] and SigLIP [82] have introduced signiﬁcant ad-
vancements. EVA uses a vanilla ViT backbone and recon-
structs visual features from masked patches, proving that
a simple masked image modeling objective can produce
powerful representations. SigLIP replaces the standard
contrastive loss with a simple sigmoid function, which im-
proves training stability and performance, especially when
scaling up the batch size. More recently, large-scale models
like InternViT [5], trained on massive web-scale data, have
demonstrated state-of-the-art performance and serve as
powerful vision backbones for MLLMs like InternVL [5].

2.2 Vision-language projector
The vision-language projector P is a critical bridge in
the MLLM architecture. Its primary objective is to trans-
form the visual patch embeddings Zv from the vision en-
coder’s feature space into the language model’s feature
space, creating projected visual embeddings Hv = P(Zv).
These aligned visual features then act as a “soft prompt”
and are fed into the language model alongside textual to-
kens. An eﬃcient projector is essential as it must perform
this alignment with minimal computational overhead and
parameter count. As proposed by Honeybee [23], eﬀective
projectors should adhere to two key design principles: (1)
adaptability to a variable number of input visual tokens
and (2) eﬃcient preservation of local spatial context. We
categorize projectors into three main types, as shown in
Fig. 5.
MLP-based method
This is the simplest and most com-

one transformation make it highly eﬃcient. This approach
excels at preserving the local context of all visual features
but lacks adaptability, as the output token count is ﬁxed
relative to the input.

This approach uses a light-

which employs a set of learnable queries to “ask” questions
of the visual features and distill them into a ﬁxed number
of output tokens. This makes it highly adaptable to vary-

cost of higher computational complexity and can some-
times weaken the explicit spatial reasoning compared to
simpler projectors. To address this issues, methods like the
D-Abstractor in Honeybee [23] use deformable attention
to maintain local context more eﬀectively.

2.4 Vision token compression
Initial research has underscored the potential of MLLMs
across various tasks, including visual question answering
and image captioning. However, MLLMs face considerable
challenges in tasks necessitating intricate recognition, in-
cluding crowd counting and optical character recognition
(OCR) of small characters. A direct approach to address-
ing these challenges involves increasing the image resolu-
tion, practically, the number of visual tokens. This strategy,
nevertheless, imposes a substantial computational burden
on MLLMs, primarily due to the quadratic scaling of com-
putational costs with the number of input tokens in the
Transformer architecture. Motivated by this challenge, vi-
sion token compression, aimed to reduce the prohibitive
computation budget caused by numerous tokens, has be-
come an essential aspect of eﬃcient MLLMs. We will ex-
plore this topic through several key techniques, including
multi-view input, token processing, multi-scale informa-
tion fusion, vision expert agents and video-speciﬁc meth-
ods.

encoders for the purpose of achieving ﬁne-grained percep-

and eﬃciency can be achieved.
Token processing
Techniques designed to process lengthy
visual token sequences are critical for eﬃcient MLLMs as
they address the dual challenges of preserving ﬁne-grained
details and reducing computational complexity. Before to-
kens are even fed to the main vision encoder, fundamental
pre-processing techniques such as downsampling or pixel
unshuﬄe are often employed. Downsampling (e.g., via av-
erage pooling or strided convolution) reduces the spatial
resolution of the image, directly cutting down the num-
ber of visual tokens. Pixel unshuﬄe is a more sophisti-
cated technique that rearranges pixels from a HR image
into a LR image with more channels, preserving all infor-
mation while making it compatible with encoders expect-
ing smaller inputs. Following these initial steps, more ad-
vanced methods are used. LLaVA-UHD [19] introduces a
novel approach to managing the computational burden as-
sociated with HR images. It incorporates two key compo-
nents: (1) a compression module that further condenses
image tokens from visual encoders, signiﬁcantly reduc-
ing computational load, and (2) a spatial schema to orga-
nize slice tokens for LLMs. Notably, LLaVA-UHD demon-
strates its eﬃciency by supporting images with resolu-
tions six times larger while using only 94% of the inference
computation required by previous models. Additionally,
the model can be eﬃciently trained in academic settings,
completing training within 23 hours on 8 A100 GPUs.
LLaVA-PruMerge [46] and MADTP [47] propose adap-
tive visual token reduction techniques that signiﬁcantly
decrease the number of visual tokens while maintaining
comparable model performance. TinyChart [44] and Tex-
tHawk [43] focus on document-oriented tasks, with the
former employing the Vision Token Merging module and
the latter introducing the ReSampling and ReArrangement
module. These modules enhance ﬁne-grained visual per-
ception and information compression capabilities. More
recently, visual token pruning has become a trending re-
search area for accelerating MLLM inference. These meth-
ods dynamically identify and discard redundant visual to-
kens before they are processed by the computationally ex-
pensive LLMs. For example, SparseVLM [96] introduces
a visual token sparsiﬁcation framework to reduce the to-
ken load. Other works propose training-free methods; Vis-
Pruner [97] leverages the attention scores related to the
[CLS] token to prune unimportant visual tokens without
any ﬁne-tuning. TopV [98] presents a compatible token
pruning method optimized for inference time speed and
low memory usage. For video-based MLLMs, where token
redundancy is even more pronounced, dynamic compres-
sion techniques have been developed. DyCoke [99] and
FastVID [100] both introduce dynamic pruning strategies
tailored for fast video LLMs, adaptively adjusting the com-
pression rate based on content complexity.
Multi-scale information fusion
The utilization of multi-
scale image information is crucial for visual feature extrac-
tion, enabling the model to capture both ﬁne-grained de-
tails at smaller scales and broader context at larger scales.
Mini-Gemini [36] features twin encoders, one for HR im-
ages and the other for LR visual embeddings. It introduces
Patch Info Mining, which employs LR visual embeddings
as queries to retrieve relevant visual cues from HR candi-
dates through cross-attention. Scaling on Scales (S2) [18]
in Fig. 6 demonstrates that a multi-scale smaller model
possesses comparable learning capacity to a larger model,

even exceed the performance of larger models on MLLM

dividing the large image into small sub-images, the S2-

that do not support window attention and avoiding the
need for training additional parameters from scratch. It
then interpolates the large feature map to the regular size,
ensuring the number of visual tokens remains acceptable.

3 Efﬁcient vision techniques
The vision encoder is a foundational component of any
MLLM, responsible for processing high-dimensional vi-
sual inputs and extracting meaningful features. Vision
Transformer (ViT) [105] architectures have become the
de facto standard for this task due to their strong perfor-
mance. However, ViTs present signiﬁcant computational
challenges. The self-attention mechanism, which is at the
core of the Transformer, has a computational and memory
cost that grows quadratically with the number of input to-
kens (i.e., image patches). As image resolution increases,
the number of tokens surges, making the vision encoder a
primary bottleneck for both inference speed and memory
usage in MLLMs.
Therefore, optimizing the vision component is not mere-
ly an independent research direction but a crucial and di-
rect pathway to achieving overall MLLM eﬃciency. Tech-
niques that make the vision encoder more compact, faster,
or less memory-intensive have a cascading positive eﬀect
on the entire MLLM pipeline. As outlined in Fig. 8, this
section explores the most prominent methods for creat-
ing eﬃcient vision models, which are directly applicable
to building lightweight MLLMs.
3.1 Compact architecture
Compact architecture refers to the design of lightweight
and eﬃcient models while maintaining high performance
in downstream tasks. It encompasses various strategies
and methodologies to reduce model size, computational
complexity, and memory footprint without compromising
performance. These strategies can be broadly categorized
into three categories, 1) architecture design methods, 2)
architecture search methods, and 3) optimization of atten-
tion mechanism methods.
Architecture design methods
Architecture design meth-
ods involve developing new architectures [106] or reﬁn-
ing existing ones [107] to enhance compactness without
compromising performance. For instance, Reformer [108]
implements locality-sensitive hashing in attention mecha-
nisms to reduce complexity and utilizes reversible residual
layers for more eﬃcient activation storage. Moreover, Eﬃ-
cientFormer [109] investigates ViT-based model architec-
tures and operators, introducing a dimension-consistent
pure Transformer paradigm and applying latency-driven
slimming to create optimized models. Additionally, Eﬃ-
cientFormerV2 [110] proposes a supernet characterized by
low latency and high parameter eﬃciency.
Architecture search methods
Architecture search meth-
ods involve employing neural architecture search algo-
rithms [111] to explore and discover compact architec-
tures tailored to speciﬁc tasks or constraints. For in-
stance, Autoformer [112] intertwines weights within lay-
ers, enabling thorough training of thousands of subnets.
NASViT [113] introduces a gradient projection algorithm,
switchable layer scaling, and streamlined data augmen-
tation, enhancing convergence and performance. Addi-
tionally, TF-TAS [114] investigates training-free archi-
tecture search methods, proposing an eﬃcient scheme.

Pruning involves removing less essential weights from Vi-

Unstructured pruning
Unstructured pruning focuses on
eliminating individual weights without considering their
structural arrangement within the model. Rao et al. [117]
introduced a dynamic token sparsiﬁcation framework for
progressive and adaptive pruning of redundant tokens
based on input. This framework integrates a lightweight
prediction module to estimate token importance scores

theoretically-grounded pruner capable of accurately and
eﬃciently handling intricate weight correlations during

Structured pruning aims to remove

3.3 Knowledge distillation
Knowledge distillation is a technique in which a smaller
model learns from a larger, more complex model to repli-
cate its performance, enabling eﬃcient deployment while
maintaining predictive accuracy [149]. Knowledge distil-
lation (KD) techniques for Vision Transformers (ViTs) can
be categorized into two main types: 1) homomorphic KDs
and 2) heteromorphic KDs.
Homomorphic KDs
Homomorphic KDs can be further
classiﬁed into logit-level [126, 127], patch-level [129],
module-level [128], and feature-level KDs [130]. For logit-
level methods, in DeiT [126], a distillation token is incor-
porated into the self-attention module to emulate the class
label inferred by the teacher model, facilitating interac-
tion between the student’s attention and layers, thus en-
abling the learning of hard labels during back-propagation.
TinyViT [127] applies distillation during pretraining,
where logits from large teacher models are pre-stored in
the hardware, enabling memory and computational eﬃ-
ciency when transferring knowledge to scaled-down stu-
dent transformers. Patch-level techniques, such as DeiT-
Tiny [129], train a small student model to match a pre-
trained teacher model on patch-level structures, and then
optimize with a decomposed manifold matching loss for
reduced computational costs. Module-level methods in-
volve segregating teacher modules from a pre-trained uni-
ﬁed model and student modules from a modular model.
In m2mKD [128], these modules are combined with a
shared meta-model, allowing the student module to em-
ulate the behavior of the teacher module. Feature-level
KD methods, as demonstrated by MiniViT [130], com-
bine the weights of consecutive transformer blocks, shar-
ing weights across layers while introducing transforma-
tions to enhance diversity. Additionally, weight distilla-
tion over self-attention is utilized to transfer knowledge
from large-scale ViT models to compact models with mul-
tiplexed weights.
Heteromorphic KDs
Heteromorphic KDs involve trans-
ferring knowledge between models with diﬀering archi-
tectures. For example, DearKD [131] proposes a novel
two-stage framework, departing from traditional methods
for ViT architectures. In the ﬁrst stage, they use a vanilla
KD strategy to transfer CNN features to the ViT student
model, representing a heteromorphic transfer. In the sub-
sequent phase, if real samples are limited, they introduce
a boundary-preserving intra-divergence loss to enhance
the process. Similarly, CiT [132] proposes a heteromor-
phic KD strategy, where knowledge is transferred from di-
verse models, such as a CNN and an involution neural net-
work, resulting in improved performance for the ViT stu-
dent model.

4.1 Attention
In the standard self-attention mechanism, the time com-
plexity is O(n2), where n is the sequence length. This
quadratic complexity arises due to the pairwise interac-
tions between all input tokens, which can lead to scalabil-
ity issues, especially when dealing with long sequences in
LLMs. To tackle these issues, researchers have developed
techniques to expedite attention mechanisms and reduce
time complexity, such as sharing-based attention, feature
information reduction, kernelization or low-rank, ﬁxed
and learnable pattern strategies, and hardware-assisted at-
tention.
Sharing-based attention
Sharing-based attention aims
to expedite attention computation during inference by
sharing computation resources across multiple key-value
heads. For example, Llama 2 [172] incorporates a tech-
nique called grouped-query attention (GQA) [152] to opti-
mize memory bandwidth during the autoregressive decod-
ing. GQA is a sharing-based attention technique that seeks
to achieve a balance between performance and eﬃciency,
positioned between multi-head attention and multi-query
attention [153] mechanisms, as illustrated in Fig. 10. In
multi-head attention, each head utilizes a distinct set of
linear transformation parameters for queries, keys, and
values. Conversely, multi-query attention shares a single
set of key-value heads across all queries. GQA partitions all
query heads into several groups, with each group’s query
heads sharing a common key-value head, thereby estab-
lishing a rigorous equilibrium between eﬀectiveness and
computational cost.
Feature information reduction
Feature information re-
duction, as evidenced by models such as Funnel-Trans-
former [154] and Set Transformer [155], addresses the cru-
cial need for computational eﬃciency in attention mecha-
nisms, speciﬁcally by reducing the dimensionality or quan-
tity of input features while preserving the essential infor-
mation embedded within the data. A key motivation be-
hind this strategy stems from the potential redundancy in
maintaining full-length hidden representations across all
layers in Transformer models. Funnel-Transformer [154]
tackles this issue by progressively reducing the sequence
size of hidden representations in self-attention models,
such as sequence length. This reduction not only decreases
computational complexity and memory usage but also
frees up resources that can be allocated toward building
deeper or wider models.
Approximate attention
Approximate attention facilitates
models to eﬃciently focus on task-relevant information
when processing long texts. Two pivotal concepts within
approximate attention are kernelization and low-rank.
Kernelization, e.g. Ref. [157], involves transforming a
problem into a kernel-based framework with the goal of
converting the original issue into a more manageable one
in a higher-dimensional space. Kernelization is primarily
employed to map text sequences into a high-dimensional
space, where task-related information can be more read-
ily captured. In this new space, each word in the text se-
quence is represented as a high-dimensional vector, and
the distances between these vectors serve to measure
their similarities. Low-rank [156] aims to decompose a
high-dimensional matrix into the product of two lower-
dimensional matrices. Consequently, by calculating the
inverses of these two lower-dimensional matrices, an ap-
proximate inverse of the attention matrix can be obtained,
thereby signiﬁcantly reducing computational complexity.
4.2 Framework
Mixture of experts
The core idea behind mixture of ex-
perts (MoE) [101] is to decompose a large-scale model into
several smaller models, each of which focuses on learn-
ing a speciﬁc part of the input data. During the training
process, each expert is assigned a weight that determines
its importance within the overall model. During the infer-
ence phase, given an input, all experts are ranked, and the
most relevant experts are selected for computation. This
approach considerably reduces the amount of computa-
tion, as only a subset of experts is involved in the calcula-
tion. By distributing computational tasks among diﬀerent
experts, MoE achieves more eﬃcient utilization of com-
putational resources during both training and inference
phases. In MoE, each expert has its own set of parameters;
however, these parameters are shared during the train-
ing process. This parameter-sharing strategy reduces the
overall number of parameters in the model, consequently
lowering storage and computational costs. GShard [158]
is a module composed of a set of lightweight annotation
APIs and XLA compiler extensions, which oﬀers an ele-
gant way to express various parallel computation patterns
while making minimal changes to existing model code. It
enables us to scale multi-lingual neural machine transla-
tion Transformer models with sparse gated mixtures of
experts to over 600 billion parameters using automatic

4.3 Fine-tuning
Fine-tuning, as the primary stage for adapting LLMs to
downstream tasks and training MLLMs to follow visual in-
structions, plays a crucial role in enhancing the eﬃciency
of LLMs.
Parameter-eﬃcient ﬁne-funing
Parameter-eﬃcient ﬁne-
tuning (PEFT) is an approach that aims to achieve high
performance with fewer parameters in LLMs. Techniques
such as adapter-based tuning and low-rank adaptation
provide eﬀective solutions to mitigate the computational
and memory challenges associated with ﬁne-tuning LLMs
while maintaining their expressiveness and generalization
capabilities. Adapter-based tuning introduces lightweight
adapter modules into the pre-trained model’s architec-
ture. These adapter modules, typically composed of feed-
forward neural networks with a small number of parame-
ters, are inserted between the layers of the original model.
During ﬁne-tuning, only the adapter parameters are up-
dated, while the pre-trained model’s parameters remain
ﬁxed. This method signiﬁcantly reduces the number of
trainable parameters, leading to faster training and in-
ference times without compromising the model’s perfor-
mance. LLM-Adapters [163] presents a framework for in-
tegrating various adapters into LLMs, enabling parameter-
eﬃcient ﬁne-tuning for diverse tasks. This framework en-
compasses state-of-the-art, openly accessible LLMs and a
wide range of widely-used adapters. (IA)3 [164] proposes a
parameter-eﬃcient ﬁne-tuning approach that learns scal-
ing vectors to modulate inner activations via multiplicative
weighting. This method enables robust few-shot learning
and supports task mixing within batches during inference,
without requiring manual adjustments to the model archi-
tecture. Low-rank adaptation [173] employs matrix factor-
ization techniques to reduce the number of parameters in
the model. By decomposing the original weight matrices
into lower-rank matrices, low-rank adaptation captures
the most signiﬁcant components of the model’s represen-
tations while discarding less important information. This
results in a more compact model with a reduced number
of parameters, which can be ﬁne-tuned more eﬃciently.
In LoRA-FA [165], a variant of LoRA, the ﬁrst low-rank
matrix is frozen after initialization and used as a random
projection, while the other is trained. This leads to a reduc-
tion in the number of parameters by half, while maintain-
ing a performance comparable to the conventional LoRA
technique. DyLoRa [166] introduces a dynamic low-rank
adaptation technique that enables the training of LoRA
blocks for a range of ranks instead of a single rank, which
is achieved by sorting the representations learned by the
adapter modules during training across diﬀerent ranks.
Full-parameter ﬁne-tuning
Full-parameter ﬁne-tuning
is an approach where all parameters of a pre-trained
model are updated during the ﬁne-tuning process. This
method aims to achieve optimal performance on a spe-
ciﬁc downstream task by leveraging the entire capacity of
the pre-trained model. While full-parameter ﬁne-tuning
often leads to state-of-the-art results and improved task-
speciﬁc performance, it comes with higher resource re-
quirements in terms of computational power and mem-
ory consumption. To alleviate the training burden, many
studies have focused on enhancing memory eﬃciency dur-
ing full-parameter ﬁne-tuning. This strategic approach
has eﬀectively diminished the obstacles that once hin-
dered progress in this ﬁeld of research. LOMO [167] in-
troduces a low-memory optimization technique derived
from stochastic gradient descent (SGD) to reduce mem-
ory consumption. Typically, the ADAM optimizer is em-
ployed; however, the optimizer states in this approach oc-
cupy a signiﬁcant amount of memory. By utilizing the
modiﬁed SGD-based LOMO, memory usage can be re-
duced. While SGD itself faces three challenges, these is-
sues tend to be resolved during model ﬁne-tuning. The
speciﬁc modiﬁcation involves updating the parameters
within the gradient computation rather than after an en-
tire layer. MeZO [168] proposes an optimizer that com-
putes gradients using merely two forward passes, enabling
the ﬁne-tuning of LLMs with a memory footprint equiva-
lent to that of inference. With a GPU memory requirement
of 55 GB, it allows for the comprehensive ﬁne-tuning of a
30-billion-parameter model.

The most common and resource-eﬃcient strat-

ponents to ﬁnd a better balance between eﬃciency and

the connector may not well align the vision and text in-

and SLM) to activate more parameters for learning better
alignment, striking a balance between full ﬁne-tuning and
a completely frozen approach. In contrast, VILA [54] takes
a more resource-intensive path, arguing that updating the
base LLM throughout the pre-training stage is essential to
inheriting some of the appealing LLM properties like in-
context learning, justifying the higher computational cost
with signiﬁcant performance gains. ShareGPT4V [60] fur-
ther demonstrates that this choice is not deﬁnite. It reveals
that unfreezing more parameters, particularly in the latter
half of the vision encoder’s layers, is advantageous when
learning larger and more diverse datasets. This ﬁnding in-
dicates that the optimal eﬃciency-performance trade-oﬀ
is data-dependent.
Data and computation-eﬃcient strategies
Beyond pa-

the multi-stage pre-training strategy used by Ideﬁcs2 [53].
To maximize computing eﬃciency, it ﬁrst pre-trains on a
massive dataset using LR images (max 384 pixels), which
allows for faster processing and larger batch sizes. Only
in a second, shorter stage does it introduce HR images
and documents. This curriculum learning approach con-
centrates the most computationally expensive tasks into
a smaller fraction of the total training time, signiﬁcantly
reducing the overall resource consumption.

the full model weights and instead facilitates the joint op-
timization of vision and language models through a small

menting LaVIN is remarkably low; for instance, it only re-
quires 1.4 training hours with 3.8 million trainable param-

5.3 Rethinking training stages for efﬁciency
Beyond optimizing individual training phases, another
key strategy for eﬃciency involves rethinking the entire
training pipeline itself. The traditional two-stage (pre-
training and instruction-tuning) paradigm is being chal-
lenged from two diﬀerent directions: consolidating stages
to reduce complexity, and designing more granular multi-
stage curricula for targeted learning.
Consolidating training stages
The traditional two-stage
strategy, which demands the manual assignment of various
adjustable parameters and dataset combinations to diﬀer-
ent training stages, can be a laborious task that introduces
signiﬁcant overhead in terms of human eﬀort and pipeline
management. To mitigate this, SPHINX-X [26] devises
a radically simpler single-stage, all-encompassing train-
ing pipeline that impartially treats all gathered datasets
and consistently converts them into multi-modal, multi-
turn dialogue formats. This approach streamlines the en-
tire process, eliminating the need for intermediate check-
points and complex stage transitions. Throughout this
uniﬁed training phase, all parameters except vision en-
coders within SPHINX-X are activated. Similarly, Co-
bra [21] argues that the initial pre-alignment phase may
not be necessary, as it introduces computational redun-
dancy and the model can remain underﬁtted even after
ﬁne-tuning. Consequently, it discards the pre-alignment
stage entirely, choosing instead to ﬁne-tune the entire lan-
guage model backbone and projector directly to maximize
the utility of every computational step.
Designing granular multi-stage curricula
In contrast to
consolidation, another approach argues that a more com-
plex but carefully designed curriculum can lead to greater
overall eﬃciency by optimizing learning at each step.
TinyGPT-V [15], for example, proposes a pipeline that
consists of four specialized stages: an initial pre-training
stage for vision-language understanding; a second stage
for reﬁning image modality processing; a third stage for
human-like learning through ﬁne-tuning; and a fourth
stage for multi-task learning to enhance its conversational
abilities as a chatbot. The eﬃciency rationale here is not
to reduce the number of stages, but to use a structured,
step-by-step curriculum where each phase uses targeted
data to build a speciﬁc capability. This strategy aims to
maximize learning eﬃciency within each phase, prevent-
ing the model from struggling with complex, mixed ob-
jectives simultaneously and potentially reaching a better
performance point with the same or fewer total resources
compared to a less structured approach.
5.4 Parameter-efﬁcient transfer learning
Parameter-eﬃcient ﬁne-tuning (PEFT) techniques are a
cornerstone of eﬃcient MLLM adaptation. They dramat-
ically reduce computational and storage costs by freez-
ing the vast majority of the model’s parameters and only
training a small number of auxiliary parameters. This not
only enables rapid, low-cost adaptation to downstream
tasks but also mitigates the catastrophic forgetting of pre-
trained knowledge. The most widely adopted method is
LoRA [173], which injects trainable low-rank matrices into
the model’s layers.
Various methods have been developed on this founda-
tion to further optimize the eﬃciency-performance trade-
oﬀ. For example, the eﬃcient attention skipping (EAS)
module [57] proposes a novel parameter and computation-
eﬃcient tuning method for MLLMs to retain high perfor-
mance and reduce both parameter and computation ex-
penditures on downstream tasks.

6 Efﬁciency-aware data and benchmarks
In the context of eﬃcient MLLMs, data and benchmarks
take on a dual role. They are not only used to measure
a model’s performance but also to quantify the resource
cost of achieving that performance. This section discusses
the datasets and evaluation protocols through the lens of
the eﬃciency-performance trade-oﬀ. We analyze how data
quality and composition can lead to more eﬃcient train-
ing, and what benchmarks are necessary to provide a holis-
tic assessment that includes not just accuracy, but also crit-
ical eﬃciency metrics such as latency, memory usage, and
computational cost.
6.1 Pre-training data
Pre-training data primarily serve two critical objectives:
(1) promoting the integration of various modalities and (2)
conveying comprehensive knowledge. From an eﬃciency
standpoint, the quality and composition of these data di-
rectly impact training cost and convergence speed. Large-
scale image-caption pair datasets, such as those listed in
Table 3, naturally fulﬁll these requirements. Firstly, these
sources are predominantly of Internet origin, providing an
extensive data volume with a broad knowledge coverage.
Secondly, the direct alignment between the two modali-
ties is beneﬁcial for training modality projectors. However,
captions in such corpora are often brief and contain noise.
These low-quality data can reduce learning eﬃciency, re-
quiring more data and longer training to achieve desired
performance. Therefore, ﬁltering these data, by employ-
ing the CLIP model to eliminate image-text pairs with low
similarity scores is a crucial ﬁrst step in improving data ef-
ﬁciency.
A key strategy to boost training eﬃciency is to use
higher-quality data. A growing number of studies have
investigated the production of high-quality ﬁne-grained
pre-trained data by leveraging powerful MLLMs like GPT-
4V. These datasets typically oﬀer more detailed and accu-
rate image descriptions compared to their coarse-grained
counterparts, enabling a closer alignment of image and
text modalities, which can allow smaller models to learn
more eﬀectively or larger models to converge faster. How-
ever, this method often requires the use of commercial
MLLMs, leading to prohibitive costs and creating an ef-
ﬁciency bottleneck in data acquisition. ShareGPT4V [60]
addresses this eﬃciency bottleneck by proposing a cost-
eﬀective data scaling strategy. It ﬁrst trains a captioner
on a small, high-quality seed dataset of 100,000 GPT-4V-
generated data and then uses this specialized, lightweight
captioner to expand the dataset to 1.2 million samples.
This amortizes the initial high cost and enables the gen-
eration of large-scale, high-quality data at a fraction of the

6.2 Instruction-tuning data
Instruction tuning (IT) is a crucial step in reﬁning eﬃcient
MLLMs’ capacity to accurately interpret user instructions
and eﬀectively carry out the desired tasks. This procedure
bears a strong connection to the concept of multi-task
prompting.
A summary of frequently used pre-training datasets can
be found in Table 4. High-quality IT data can be derived
from task-speciﬁc datasets. For instance, consider a sam-
ple from VQA datasets where the input includes an im-
age and a natural language question, and the output is
the text-based answer to the question based on the im-
age. This could easily form the multimodal input and re-
sponse of the instruction sample. The instructions, or
task descriptions, can be obtained either through man-
ual creation or semi-automatic generation with the help of
GPT. In addition to utilizing publicly available task-speciﬁc
datasets, SPHINX-X [26] assembles a dataset focused on
OCR from a wide range of PDF data sourced from the In-
ternet. Speciﬁcally, it begins by gathering a large-scale PDF
dataset from the web. It then obtains the rendering results
of each page in the PDF ﬁle, while simultaneously saving
all text annotations along with their respective bounding
boxes. Ultimately, these elements are converted into a uni-
ﬁed question-answering format.
While multi-task datasets provide an abundant source
of data, they may not always be suitable for complex real-
world situations, such as engaging in multi-turn conver-
sations. To address this challenge, some research has ex-
plored the use of self-instruction by leveraging LLMs to
generate text-based or multimodal instruction-following
data from a limited number of manually annotated sam-
ples.
SPHINX-X [26] assembles a rich multi-domain dataset
with ﬁne-grained correspondence between images and
texts. It gathers images from diverse sources and then em-
ploys annotations to apply various markers onto the orig-
inal images. By prompting GPT-4V with these marked
images and tailored domain-speciﬁc guidelines, the sys-
tem generates captions that oﬀer an image overview, re-
gional details, and insights into object relationships. Dur-
ing the training process, SPHINX-X utilizes the unaltered
images rather than the marked ones to describe the mark-
ers through language within interactive conversations to
ensure consistency across multiple data domains.
ALLaVA [38] proposes to distill a caption and a question-
answer (QA) pair for an image within a single session.
Speciﬁcally, it prompts GPT-4V with an image and asks it
to ﬁrst generate a ﬁne-grained caption, followed by a visual
question-answer (VQA) pair.

6.3 Benchmarks
With the aim of delivering an all-encompassing perfor-
mance evaluation, we have assembled a table that demon-
strates the eﬀectiveness of 22 MLLMs across 14 well-
established VL benchmarks, as depicted in Table 5. Addi-

In recent years, the evaluation landscape has expanded
to include more challenging and comprehensive bench-
marks. For instance, MMMU [201] is a new benchmark
designed to evaluate models on college-level problems
requiring expert knowledge across various domains. For
tasks requiring ﬁne-grained text recognition, OCR-
Bench [205] provides a robust testbed for evaluating opti-
cal character recognition capabilities in diverse scenes. For
understanding structured data visualizations, benchmarks
such as ChartQA [206] and DocVQA [182] are essential

documents. Furthermore, comprehensive evaluation plat-
forms like OpenCompass [207] have emerged, oﬀering a
standardized suite to test a wide array of models across
numerous benchmarks, providing a holistic view of their
capabilities.
For video-based tasks, which are inherently more re-
source-intensive, specialized benchmarks are crucial.
MeViS [208, 209], for example, provides a large-scale
benchmark for video segmentation that speciﬁcally evalu-
ates temporal and motion understanding, oﬀering critical
insights into how well models generalize in dynamic, mul-
timodal settings.
7 Applications
From the preceding analysis, it is clear that many eﬃcient
MLLM approaches evaluate their performances across a
range of scenarios, such as VQA, visual grounding, and
image segmentation [210]. However, it is also crucial to
explore these eﬃcient architectures in well-established
tasks to achieve their ultimate performance. Therefore, we
have chosen to introduce several downstream tasks, such
as medical analysis, document understanding, and video
comprehension.
7.1 Biomedical analysis
Due to the high cost of annotating biomedical data, foun-
dation models are poised to become a new paradigm in
biomedicine, achieving state-of-the-art results on many
applications, including medical question answering [211]
and medical image classiﬁcation [212]. Recently, multi-
modal generative AI has emerged as an exciting frontier in
the biomedical domain, expanding the application scope
from single-modality to multi-modality, such as VQA and
radiology report generation.
The mixture of expert tuning has eﬀectively enhanced
the performance of general MLLMs with fewer parame-
ters, yet its application in resource-limited medical set-
tings has not been fully explored. Med-MoE [69] is a model
tailored for medical applications that signiﬁcantly lower
parameter demands. LLaVA-Rad [68] is a state-of-the-art
tool that demonstrates rapid performance on a single V100
GPU in private settings, making it highly applicable for
real-world clinical scenarios. It employs a modular ap-
proach, integrating unimodal pre-trained models and em-
phasizing the training of lightweight adapters. As a result,
LLaVA-Rad outperforms larger models such as GPT-4V
and Med-PaLM in terms of standard metrics, showcasing
its superior eﬃciency and eﬀectiveness.
7.2 Document understanding
Documents or charts serve as a crucial source of infor-
mation, oﬀering an intuitive visualization of data in vari-
ous forms. They have become an indispensable part of in-
formation dissemination, business decision-making, and
academic research. However, current chart understanding
models still face two primary limitations: (1) The consid-
erable number of parameters makes training and deploy-
ment challenging. For instance, ChartLlama [213], a 13-
billion-parameter model, is diﬃcult to deploy on a single
consumer-grade GPU. (2) These models struggle with ef-
ﬁciently encoding HR images, as vision transformers tend
to produce lengthy feature sequences.
To address the challenges of ﬁne-grained visual percep-
tion and visual information compression for document-
oriented MLLMs, TinyChart [44] outperforms several
13-billion-parameter MLLMs with program-of-thoughts
(PoT) learning and visual token merging strategy while
excelling in faster inference speed at the same time. Tex-
tHawk [43] explores eﬃcient ﬁne-grained perception by
designing four dedicated components to address chal-
lenges posed by document-oriented tasks. HRVDA [71]
and Monkey [70] are also large multimodal models de-
signed to address the challenges posed by HR require-
ments in visual document understanding tasks.

age LLMs to create end-to-end chat-centric video com-
prehension systems. However, these methods are limited
to processing a restricted number of frames, which con-
strains their ability to understand longer videos.
To address the computational challenges associated with
processing long videos due to the excessive number of
visual tokens, several approaches have been developed.
mPLUG-video [72] is designed for video understanding
tasks. It begins with a TimeSformer-based video encoder
to extract features from sparsely sampled video frames
eﬀectively, followed by a visual abstractor module to re-
duce sequence length. Video-LLaVA [49] excels in vari-
ous video understanding tasks by unifying visual repre-
sentations of images and videos into a single language fea-
ture space before projection. This approach enables eﬀec-
tive learning of multi-modal interactions with Language-
Bind [103]. LLaMA-VID [74] addresses this issue by repre-
senting each frame with two distinct tokens, namely con-
text token and content token. The context token encodes
the overall image context based on user input, whereas
the content token encapsulates visual cues in each frame.
This dual-token strategy signiﬁcantly reduces the overload
of long videos while preserving critical information. In-
stead of trying to process more frames simultaneously like
most existing work, MA-LMM [73] proposes to process
videos in an online manner and store past video informa-
tion in a memory bank to reference historical video con-
tent for long-term analysis without exceeding LLMs’ con-
text length constraints or GPU memory limits.
7.4 Autonomous driving
Autonomous driving represents a critical real-world appli-
cation where MLLMs can play a transformative role. Ve-
hicles are equipped with a suite of sensors (cameras, Li-
DAR, radar) that generate a continuous stream of multi-
modal data. Eﬃcient MLLMs are being explored to pro-
cess these data for high-level scene understanding, reason-
ing, and decision-making [75]. For example, an MLLM can
interpret a complex traﬃc scene by describing the rela-
tionships between vehicles, pedestrians, and traﬃc signals
in natural language (“the pedestrian is about to cross the
street against a red light”). This enables more transparent
and interpretable decision-making for the vehicle’s control
system, bridging the gap between black-box models and
human-understandable reasoning [76]. The eﬃciency of
these models is paramount, as low-latency inference is a
strict requirement for on-road safety.
7.5 Remote sensing
Remote sensing, which involves the analysis of data from
satellites and aerial imagery, is another promising domain
for eﬃcient MLLMs [77–79]. These models can be used
for tasks such as land use classiﬁcation, environmental
monitoring, change detection after natural disasters, and
agricultural yield prediction. For example, an MLLM could
analyze a time-series of satellite images and generate a
textual summary of deforestation in a speciﬁc region or
identify areas aﬀected by ﬂooding. The ability of eﬃcient
MLLMs to process large-scale visual data and provide se-
mantic interpretations makes them a powerful tool for
scientists and policymakers, enabling faster and more in-
sightful analysis of our planet [216].
8 Discussion
8.1 Comparative analysis and practical insights
This survey has categorized a wide array of techniques for
building eﬃcient MLLMs. A critical analysis reveals that
there is no one-size-ﬁts-all solution; instead, the most ef-
fective approach depends on the speciﬁc application’s con-
straints and performance targets. We draw the following
conclusions:
1) Architecture co-design is critical. The most success-
ful eﬃcient MLLMs, such as MobileVLM V2 [16]
and MoE-LLaVA [20], demonstrate a balanced, co-
designed approach. The choice of vision encoder, pro-
jector, and language model backbone are not inde-
pendent decisions. For instance, a simple MLP pro-
jector is the most eﬃcient in terms of parameters and
latency but may struggle with complex spatial reason-
ing tasks. In contrast, attention-based projectors like
Q-Former [88] oﬀer better performance at the cost of
increased complexity. The optimal choice is therefore
highly conditional on the target application’s needs.
2) The trade-oﬀof using HR inputs should be carefully
considered. While techniques like vision token com-
pression are essential for processing HR images with-
out prohibitive computational costs, they inherently
introduce a trade-oﬀwith ﬁne-grained detail recogni-
tion. Methods like S2-Wrapper [18] oﬀer a pragmatic
balance by enabling the use of pre-trained models on
scaled sub-images, but tasks requiring meticulous de-
tail (e.g., OCR on small text) may still suﬀer.
3) Training strategy matters. For scaling up model ca-
pacity without a proportional increase in inference
cost, mixture-of-experts (MoE) tuning, as seen in
MoE-LLaVA [20], has proven highly eﬀective. How-
ever, for achieving the best possible performance on a
compact model, studies like VILA [54] show that par-
tially or fully unfreezing the language model during
pre-training is more eﬀective than only training the
projector, as it allows for better cross-modal align-
ment.
In summary, the prevailing trend for achieving eﬃciency
without a catastrophic performance loss involves a careful
combination of a lightweight language model (e.g., Phi-2,
Gemma), an eﬃcient projector (e.g., LDPv2), and an ad-
vanced training strategy (e.g., MoE-Tuning).

8.2 Limitations and future work
The development of eﬃcient MLLMs is still in its nascent
stage, and there is ample room for improvement. We sum-
marize the current state of research as follows:
1) At present, eﬃcient MLLMs face challenges in pro-
cessing extended-context multimodal information,
and they are typically limited to accepting single im-
ages. This constrains the advancement of more so-
phisticated models capable of handling an increased
number of multimodal tokens. Such models would
be beneﬁcial for applications such as comprehending
lengthy videos and analyzing extensive documents
that incorporate a mix of images and text, creating
more versatile and powerful systems.
2) The predominant eﬃcient MLLMs mainly support
dual input modalities—images and texts, and a sin-
gular output modality—text. However, the tangible
world encompasses a more extensive array of modali-
ties. By expanding the scope of eﬃcient MLLMs to ac-
commodate a richer diversity of input modalities, and
augmenting their generative capacities, we can sig-
niﬁcantly bolster their multifunctionality and widen
their applicability.
3) There are two principal pathways to fortify eﬃcient
MLLM models. Firstly, the incorporation of a more
varied set of lightweight LLMs can render the de-
sign of MLLMs more adaptable, facilitating their cus-
tomization to cater to a broad spectrum of require-
ments. Secondly, leveraging high-quality instruction
tuning datasets can empower eﬃcient MLLMs to bet-
ter comprehend and implement a vast array of in-
structions, thereby amplifying their zero-shot learn-
ing capabilities.
4) The development of embodied agents capable of de-
ployment on edge devices represents a crucial ap-
plication prospect for eﬃcient MLLMs. An agent
possessing specialized knowledge and the capability
to interact with the real world has far-reaching im-
plications, potentially revolutionizing ﬁelds such as
robotics, automation, and artiﬁcial intelligence.
5) A signiﬁcant gap exists between demonstrating eﬃ-
ciency on academic benchmarks and successful de-
ployment on edge devices. The practical challenges
of on-device inference, such as strict hardware con-
straints (e.g., limited RAM and specialized NPUs
on smartphones), power consumption limits, and
the need for low latency, are often under-discussed.
While models like MobileVLM [16] are designed for
mobile scenarios, there is a lack of comprehensive
case studies that detail the full deployment pipeline,
including the impact of quantization (e.g., INT8 or
lower), pruning, and compilation for speciﬁc hard-
ware targets. Future research would greatly beneﬁt
from more practical evaluations on real-world edge
hardware, reporting metrics such as inference speed
and energy usage to bridge the gap between theoreti-
cal eﬃciency and practical applicability.
6) Finally, while this survey focuses on visual under-
standing and reasoning tasks, a related and rapidly
growing application of MLLMs is multimodal-guided
image editing, as surveyed in Ref. [217]. Developing
eﬃcient versions of these generative models for on-
device use presents another promising research direc-
tion.
9 Conclusion
In this study, we take a deep dive into the realm of ef-
ﬁcient MLLM literature, providing an all-encompassing
view of its central themes, including foundational theories
and their extensions. Our goal is to identify and highlight
areas that require further research and suggest potential
avenues for future studies. This paper provides a compre-
hensive perspective on the current state of research on ef-
ﬁcient MLLM, with the hope of inspiring future research
in this ﬁeld. Our review indicates that a prevailing trend
for achieving eﬃciency without catastrophic performance
loss involves a combination of lightweight language mod-
els (e.g., Phi-2, Gemma), eﬃcient projectors (e.g., LDPv2),
and advanced training strategies like MoE-Tuning. While
methods such as token compression are crucial for HR in-
puts, they often introduce a trade-oﬀwith ﬁne-grained de-
tail recognition. The most eﬀective methods in practice,
such as MobileVLM V2 [16] and MoE-LLaVA [20], demon-
strate a balanced approach, carefully co-designing the ar-
chitecture and training pipeline for a speciﬁc eﬃciency-
performance target. Given the dynamic nature of this ﬁeld,
it is possible that some recent developments may not be
fully covered. To address this issue, we have set up a dedi-
cated website that uses crowdsourcing to keep up with the
latest advancements. This platform is intended to serve as
a continually updated source of information, promoting
ongoing growth in the ﬁeld. Due to space constraints, we
cannot cover all technical details in depth but have pro-
vided brief overviews of the key contributions in the ﬁeld.
In the future, we plan to continuously update and enhance
the information on our website, with the addition of new
insights as they come to light.

Abstract: In the past years, multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have demonstrated remarkable performance in tasks such as visual question answering and visual understanding and reasoning. However, the extensive model size and high training and inference costs have hindered the widespread application of MLLMs in academia and industry. Thus, studying eﬃcient and lightweight MLLMs has enormous potential, especially in edge computing scenarios. In this survey, we provide a comprehensive and systematic review of the current state of eﬃcient MLLMs. Speciﬁcally, this survey summarizes the timeline of representative eﬃcient MLLMs, the current state of research in structures and strategies, and the applications. Finally, the limitations of current eﬃcient MLLM research and promising future directions are discussed.
